learn.title: 17 · Reference solution

designClaim: fill a from the back with the larger of the two current tails; stop when b is used up — O(m + n) time, O(1) memory
solutionMd:
## The idea

If we merged from the front we would overwrite numbers in `a` that we still need. The free space is at the **end**, so fill from the back: the largest remaining number goes into the last free slot.

## Step by step

1. i = last real value in a, j = last value in b, write = last slot.
2. While b still has values: put the larger of a[i] and b[j] at `write` and step that pointer back.
3. When b is empty, stop — what remains of a is already in place.

## Worked example

**Input:** a = [1,2,3,_,_,_], b = [2,5,6]

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 6 vs 3 | write 6 |
| 5 vs 3 | write 5 |
| 2 vs 3 | write 3 |
| 2 vs 2 | take b's 2 (a's is not larger) |
| b has nothing left | stop; a's 1, 2 are already in place |

**Result:** [1,2,2,3,5,6]

## Cost

O(m + n) time, O(1) extra memory.

## The code (C#, compiled and tested against every part of the question)

```csharp
// LeetCode 88 — merge sorted b into sorted a, in place. a has room for both (length m + n).
public static class MergeSorted {
    public static void Merge(int[] a, int m, int[] b, int n) {
        // Fill a from the BACK. The free space is at the end, so nothing we still need is overwritten.
        int i = m - 1, j = n - 1, write = m + n - 1;
        while (j >= 0) {                                 // once b is used up, a's front is already in place
            if (i >= 0 && a[i] > b[j]) a[write--] = a[i--];
            else a[write--] = b[j--];
        }
    }
}
```

## Likely follow-up questions

**Q: What if b runs out first?**

**Q: Complexity?**

O(m + n) time, O(1) extra.

**Q: Shared state?**

It mutates a — the caller must not read it concurrently.

**Q: Merge k sorted arrays.**

A min-heap of the k heads: O(N log k).

**Q: Merge two sorted files too big for memory.**

Stream both, write the merged output — the external merge-sort step.
